concepts.def: Sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound is ordinary sound — a longitudinal wave that needs a medium — and differs from audible sound only in having a frequency too high for the human ear to detect.

The surface where one material meets a different material, for example soft tissue meeting bone, or one rock layer meeting another. Because the two materials carry the wave differently, a wave arriving at a boundary is changed there rather than passing through unaffected.

When a wave meets a boundary between two different media, part of the wave is reflected back and the rest carries on into the second medium. Ultrasound is partially reflected at every boundary it meets, which is why a single pulse can return several reflections from several depths.

The transfer of energy from a wave to the material it is passing through, so the wave becomes weaker as it travels. Different materials absorb a given wave by different amounts, and how strongly a signal has been weakened is itself information about what the wave has passed through.

The speed at which a wave travels is a property of the wave in a particular material, not of the wave alone. The same wave travels at different speeds in different materials, and it is this difference in velocity at a boundary that produces a reflection and reveals a hidden structure.

Using high frequency sound waves to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth. A pulse is sent downwards, the time until its echo returns is measured, and the depth is found from that time — remembering that the pulse has travelled down and back.

A wave produced by an earthquake that travels through the Earth. Seismic waves are detected far from the earthquake, and which types arrive where is evidence about the material they have passed through.

A longitudinal seismic wave. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so the times and directions in which they arrive carry information about the material deep inside the Earth.
A transverse seismic wave. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so a region of the Earth that receives no S-waves after an earthquake indicates liquid material somewhere on the path.

The central region of the Earth, which no one has ever seen or sampled. P-waves and S-waves provide the evidence for its structure and its size: S-waves failing to arrive shows liquid material, and the changing speed of P-waves shows where the core begins.

Evidence about something that cannot be observed directly, obtained by measuring what a wave does after passing near or through it. Ultrasound imaging, industrial testing and the study of the Earth's interior all rest on indirect evidence of this kind.

The use of ultrasound to build a picture of a structure hidden from view — an unborn baby or an organ in medicine, a crack or a flaw inside a metal casting in industry. Each reflection detected is turned into the distance to a boundary, and the set of distances becomes the image.

mcqs.q: A survey team sends waves down into the ground to look for a buried rock layer in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens when the waves reach the top of that buried layer?
options: The waves carry on downwards at exactly the same speed
Part of each wave is reflected back and the rest travels on
All of each wave is reflected and none of it travels on
The waves are all absorbed at the top of the buried layer
mcqs.explain: A change of velocity at a boundary between two different media produces a partial reflection. The reflected part returns to the detector and reveals the layer; the transmitted part carries on and can reflect from deeper boundaries.

mcqs.q: Survey waves pass easily through rock layer X but are strongly absorbed by rock layer Y. How does this difference help the team explore ground they cannot see?
options: A weak returning signal shows the waves went through layer Y
Strong absorption sends back a stronger reflection from layer Y
Layer Y reflects every wave, so nothing returns from below
Both layers return the same signal, so absorption is no use
mcqs.explain: How much a signal has been weakened is itself information. Waves that come back weak have passed through the strongly absorbing rock, so the strength of each returning signal maps out where each type of rock lies.

mcqs.q: Which statement about ultrasound waves is correct?
options: Their frequency is below the lowest frequency a person hears
They are electromagnetic waves, like the X-rays used in hospitals
They are ordinary sound waves that are simply far too quiet to hear
Their frequency is above the highest frequency a person hears
mcqs.explain: The specification states that ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. They remain sound waves in every other respect.

mcqs.q: An ultrasound pulse travelling through soft tissue meets a boundary with bone. What happens to the pulse at that boundary?
options: All of it bounces back and none enters the bone
None of it comes back; it all enters the bone
Part of it is reflected, part carries on
It is absorbed there and turned into heat
mcqs.explain: The specification says ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media. The reflected part times that boundary; the rest travels on to the next one.

mcqs.q: An ultrasound pulse leaves a probe on a patient's skin and travels at 1500 m/s. The reflection from a boundary inside the body is detected 0.001 s after the pulse leaves the probe. How far is that boundary from the probe?
options: 3 m
mcqs.explain: Distance travelled = speed × time = 1500 × 0.001 = 1.5 m. That is the there-and-back path, so the boundary is half of it away: 0.75 m.

mcqs.q: A ship measures water depth by echo sounding. It records the time between sending a sound pulse downwards and detecting the echo. How is the depth found from that time?
options: Multiply the time by the speed of sound in water
Divide the speed of sound in water by that time
Halve the time, multiply by the speed, halve again
Multiply the time by the speed of sound, then halve it
mcqs.explain: Speed × time gives the whole path the pulse travelled, down to the sea bed and back. The depth is half of that. Halving the time first and then multiplying would be equally correct.

mcqs.q: Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves rather than light or radio waves. Why is sound the wave that is used?
options: Sound travels faster through deep sea water than light does
Water absorbs light and radio waves in a short distance
Any wave would work here; sound is just the usual choice
Sound is the only wave the sea bed can reflect back
mcqs.explain: This is the use of absorption the specification asks students to explain. Light and radio waves do not survive the journey to the sea bed and back; high frequency sound does, so it can carry the information.

mcqs.q: Which statement about P-waves and S-waves is correct?
options: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal
Both P-waves and S-waves are longitudinal waves
P-waves are longitudinal, S-waves transverse
Both P-waves and S-waves are transverse waves
mcqs.explain: The specification states that P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves and S-waves are transverse, seismic waves. It is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid.

mcqs.q: After an earthquake, detectors on the far side of the Earth record P-waves but no S-waves. What does this indicate about the Earth's core?
options: No seismic wave of any kind can pass through the core
There is an empty gap inside the Earth stopping the S-waves
S-waves are too weak to reach any detector that far away
Part of the core is liquid: S-waves cannot pass through liquid
mcqs.explain: The specification states that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid. Their absence on the far side, while P-waves still arrive, is the evidence that part of the core is liquid.

mcqs.q: P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. How does this provide evidence about the Earth's core?
options: Where their speed changes shows where the core begins and ends
P-waves keep one fixed speed, so arrival times give distance only
P-waves are absorbed by the core, so a shadow shows its size
P-waves cannot enter the core, so nothing arrives beyond it
mcqs.explain: A change of speed marks a change of material. Tracking where P-waves speed up or slow down, and where they arrive, gives evidence for both the structure and the size of the core.

mcqs.q: A P-wave travels through solid rock. How does the rock itself move as the wave passes through it?
options: The rock is carried bodily along with the wave as it travels
The rock moves from side to side across the direction of travel
The rock vibrates back and forth in the direction of travel
The rock stays perfectly still while the wave passes
mcqs.explain: P-waves are longitudinal, so the oscillations of the rock are parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. The rock returns to its position; only energy moves on.

mcqs.q: The study of seismic waves led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable. What did the seismic waves provide?
options: Confirmation of what deep drilling had already shown
Evidence about material that nobody has seen
Ideas about the deep Earth that can never be tested
A direct view of the core through the rock above
mcqs.explain: The waves pass through regions no one can observe and carry information back out. That indirect evidence is what led to the discoveries about the Earth's interior.
